utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The witness, please. Mr. Kovacic, we'll go on until 4.15, if we start now, take a break for a quarter of an hour then, and then we'll have an hour's further hearing and finish at half past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, I understand. But perhaps this is a good time, since we're talking about that, I need to apologise to the Court. When you asked me on Thursday, I said I would need about an hour to complete this, but one whole topic somehow was hidden among my papers, and I do think that I shall need two, two and a half hours, if we proceed as you just told us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Zlotrg.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to adduce into evidence D4/2, which was not translated into English last week. Meanwhile, we received the translation, so that I should like to -- if I may remind you, that is the record of the investigation on site. It was only in Serbo-Croatian, and now we also have the English translation of it. Witness, let us try and save some time. On Thursday, we talked at great length about disorder in the town, if I may call it, quite a number of crimes, et cetera, and we mentioned also other units which were there, that is, men who were there. Do you remember a group of Herzegovinians of the HVO who were there and who were called Herzegovinians there?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was a regular unit of the Croatian Defence Council which however had marks on its shoulder of unity, and they were quartered at the elementary school in Dubrovica. And they took shifts, so the units took shifts. It was the same unit, but other companies would come.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. But are you aware that that unit or rather its men came from outside the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but they were members of the Croatian Defence Council. Yes, right, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But tell us, "Yes" or "No", did they come from outside the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You have to say it, because on the record it doesn't show when you nod your head.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know if they all came from outside the municipality of Vitez, but there were quite a number of men that I did not know. Where they came from, I do not know. I mean I really don't know where they came from, because we had no access to them. We did not talk to them, we had no contact with them. They simply engaged in terrorising the population of Muslim origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that some people -- or at least have you heard of the name that people call them, Herzegovinians?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) At this point in time, I should like to tender another document into evidence. It was already tendered in the Blaskic case. Unfortunately, Judge Bennouna, as again I do not have the French translation, I did ask for the French translation, and I thought it would be here, but it was not. But I can ask for it, if you like, later on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D10/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, I should first like to draw your attention to the person who signed the document. Is it the same person, Ivan Budimir, that we talked about so far?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot say anything from the signature. I do not know the signature of Ivan Budimir. But from what is printed above, I presume it is him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Will you please look at item 2 of the document? Does the wording of item 2 correspond with the situation that was there? Does it fit into the picture that you described to us?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but it was a small unit. It was subordinated to a superior command. That is, it was subordinated to the command commanded by -- to the commander, Ivan Budimir, since it is his signature. And we have the brigade commander, and the military commander was responsible for suppressing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, how do you know that that unit was subordinated under the command of the same unit which -- to which Mr. Cerkez also belonged to?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, following some military doctrine, a smaller unit arriving in the territory of a larger unit is to be subordinated to its command, to the command of the larger unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But on Thursday, you told us that you knew nothing about military rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not of the HVO, but I know how it is in the Armija, and I suppose that that is the case of all armies. And at any rate, look at the films. You will see always that when a unit comes into the territory of the local unit, they'll be subordinated to it, if, of course, the local unit is larger. That is my assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One moment. It's not working.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it is your assumption; you are not certain about that?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It's a rule. And you told us that you were not conversant with the internal issue or structure? "Yes" or "No", please.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So we can proceed. You also spoke, in relation to the subject about the accused [indiscernible], they trained in the town at the time later in '92 to late '93, and I shall quote to you an example, another note by Mr. Budimir, and I shall ask you if you know something about that particular event. And this is another document I wish to tender. Will the usher please take care of that? This is another document which was used in the Blaskic case. Judge Bennouna, you wouldn't believe it, but there is a translation of this particular document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: D11/2, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask you two questions with regard to this document, and please answer me only "Yes" or "No" just to speed matters up. We do not need any explanation. First, I should like to ask you something about the first part of the document, where we have those items 1 and 2 with the introductory sentence, and the paragraph just below. Could you read that, please?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is a hand-held rocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Such events, do they remind of you some other incidents that you mentioned that had been happening around the town? Could one say that this was one of the incidents that happened?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does it perhaps remind you of some of the incidents that you listed among your reports, 37 or something?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The answer is "evidently, no." The interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So, this incident happened later?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: The answer, this is not reported our station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Zoran Krizanovic is a Bosniak or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So there were some Croats who suffered damage at least in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but if this is the time there about, this is very scant information, and there were eyewitnesses of when Zolja was fired, and Croat eyewitnesses, and unfortunately they say it was Croats who fired this Zolja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, just a moment, Witness, please. All I'm asking you, does this show that some Croats were victimised too? I wasn't asking you where the Zolja came from, nor let it imply that. Does the name Zoran Krizanovic tell you that he was a Croat?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No. Please, I mean, only "yes" without "but" or anything. Does this also tell you that it is a record here that the Croat [indiscernible] the damage also?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about who attacked him. The other party can ask you.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: A disobedient Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And although explosive devices were thrown in different places, we do not know who suffered damage, I mean, who were the owners of objects that were damaged?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is what this report says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In keeping with what you told us, these are evidently incidents which were reported in the part of the town under the control of the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the examination-in-chief, you said, among other things, and I shall try to quote you, you said on the 8th of January, '93, in front of the Public Security Station in Vitez, the Croatian flag was hoisted and the flag of Bosnia-Herzegovina was taken down. I emphasise, you said it was on the 8th of January, '93, so it is the very beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, that is a mistake. On the 21st or, rather, towards the end of November, we formed the station in Stari Vitez, and in October, when we were driven out, in '92, that is when the Croatian flag was hoisted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So this was October, '92. All right. I apologise. Tell me, please, so you are relating this flag to events of October?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, at the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. So which flag of Bosnia-Herzegovina was taken down? Will you please tell us what flag was that?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it is -- this is obviously -- there was either a misinterpretation or some misunderstanding. There is -- at the checkpoint at the railway station, I would have to go through my notes now, in 1992, it was a mixed checkpoint of civilian police and military police forces. Then if I'm correct, Vladimir Jukic led the group when members of the Croatian Defence Council and the Croatian police drove away all members of the Muslim nationality and took down the flag of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the white flag with lilies, and left the Croatian flag. On the building of the police station in Vitez, as far as I know, the flag of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina has never been hoisted there because Croatian gentlemen were rather irritated by that, and we simply did not put it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let's leave it at that. You said that a white flag with lilies was taken down. That was the flag of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm describing it. In October 1992, the flag of Bosnia-Herzegovina, white lilies. Tell us, please, what decision -- why is it the official flag? Why do you say it is the official flag of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Who proclaimed it the flag of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that I perceived it as my own. I know that it was hoisted in front of the United Nations buildings. I know that the whole world recognised it, and that the Croats refused to recognise it, well, there's nothing I can do about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What about the other ethnic groups of Bosnia and Herzegovina, did they consider this to be their own flag of Bosnia-Herzegovina too, for example, the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know when the official flag of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established as such by the relevant decision or the relevant body of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: You would have to ask a politician that question. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I don't think we're going to be much assisted with this line of argument. Can we move on, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, I'm finished with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Among other things, when you were telling us about the time when you could not work as a policeman because you were driven out of the station, you hadn't established the new one in Stari Vitez yet, you mentioned at one point that in November 1992, you carried out an on-site investigation in connection with the killing of two members of the Territorial Defence, and you were there as a criminology technician. You were there simply to assist the military police of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, then I have two questions in that regard. Were you paid for that work?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You did that on a voluntary basis?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was that perhaps work duty that was proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, I was an employee of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did the military police have a criminology technician at the time, the TO military police?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Wasn't Mr. Ramo Vatres their criminology technician?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Ramo Vatres was head of the criminology department, and he was an inspector.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was he a qualified criminology technician by training, though?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you would have to ask him. Really, I don't know. I know that he was involved in operations, but whether he was a technician by training, that, I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You did not work with him before that in the police?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. At that time, we're talking about November 1992, you claim that that organisation was still called the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Please, don't take my word as far as dates are concerned. I really don't know when these names were changed. And then, after all, it was after the pressure exerted by the Croatian side that the TO changed its name. They were simply seeking ways and means of preventing a united army from existing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Please, could you just give me "Yes" or "No" answers? Could you tell us at least approximately when the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was founded? Give us the season of the year, at least.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. We were very busy in terms of organising the police station. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's an answer too. Thank you. Now I would like to put a few questions to you in relation to Mr. Cerkez, whom you mentioned. So let's try to go through all of this as quickly as possible. You said that Cerkez, before the JNA aggression began against Bosnia and Herzegovina, rather, against the Serbs, he worked in the SPS in a similar job as you did in the police.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I imagine it was similar to my work. What he exactly did, that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps whether this similar work was some kind of an executive position in the SPS or was he a clerk of sorts or what was he?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, it wasn't really a management job, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell us, you even mentioned Mr. Cerkez's mother. You said that she worked as a cashier in a shop. Are you sure that this was in a shop?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, she worked at the department store.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: At the department store.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Are you sure it's the department store?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, because I've known this woman since I was a young boy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Cerkez's mother and father. However, you didn't say more about that. Did you know them better? You said that you repaired the father's car, so you knew them.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, Cerkez worked at the post office. He was a PTT mechanic, if I'm not mistaken. He was involved, that is to say, in telephones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have the impression that that family as a family had a nationalist view of things, that they treated people differently in terms of their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, because he wouldn't have been friends with my sister-in-law who is a Serb and my brother-in-law who is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that Mario Cerkez had a very good relationship with your late brother?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were not family friends, but they did have a good relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were they involved in sports together?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in view of the post held by Mario Cerkez in the HVO command, as you said, at the hotel, what do you know about that? First of all, who was staying at the hotel at the time, for example, in mid 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: We were not allowed access to the hotel, so according to what I heard when I talked to Croats, I imagined that he did hold a command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of an institution called the municipal staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No. No, I told you a few minutes ago, we had many problems within the police. We were driven out twice, and then there were questions of organisation, et cetera, but I said that he was commander of the staff. I don't know whether it was the municipal staff or the staff of the brigade, because I said even then that I did not know his exact post, and I was not familiar with the organisational structure of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear anything about Cerkez being in Novi Travnik at a given point in time?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that he was a candidate. I think that Zeljko Sajevic was supposed to be there, Zeljko Sajevic from Vitez, and Cerkez, and I was surprised when I heard that Cerkez went to the command, because Sajevic was a member of the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence. He was a worker, rather. And when the commander of the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence was away, then he would replace him, and I thought that Sajevic would be in this joint command. I don't know the exact period. I'm just telling you about what I heard when I talked to Croats, and you can probably look at the records of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, you know that Cerkez was in Novi Travnik, in the command there?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of what I managed to hear from my Croat friends, because our movement in Vitez was restricted, let alone going to Travnik. I mean, that would have been lunacy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We're talking about November 1992, the beginning of that period?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Even then, even then, the members of the Croatian Defence Council will take away my official pass even and look at it in Nevic Polje, and it was not really a good idea for Muslims to move around because a lot of them ended up locked up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Since you mentioned Mr. Sajevic, you said that he was a candidate, but you don't know what kind of a candidate. Do you know that he was a member of the same command in Novi Travnik with Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I really don't know. I also don't think that Cerkez knows what was going on in our command, so, I mean, I was not a member of this staff, so I think it is pointless to ask me anything related to their establishments, and dates when persons were appointed to posts there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are means, but then you mentioned that you knew what Cerkez did in Vitez, so perhaps you also knew what he did there?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: All of these are just assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I have a few questions to put to you in relation to the distinctions in terms of the HVO. You keep talking about the HVO, but I want to put a concrete question to you, and please be as brief as possible. You mentioned explicitly the military police of the HVO. Do you know anything about who the commander of this unit was?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that at the outset, Budimir was the commander. He transferred from Bila, as far as I know, and he's also mentioned in the record that was made by the judge when Trako Samir was murdered. If I'm not mistaken, Budimir himself introduced himself as the commander of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps what rank this unit of the military police had? Was it a battalion? Was it a company? Oh, you don't know? Well, okay, you don't know?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know the words that you're using for battalion and other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. But you know that there was a separate unit of the military police?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that there was a company, and I know that there was a brigade, military police, but the word you mentioned for battalion, I have never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps during 1992 where the command of the military police was?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know when we were working on the murder of those two members in Kruscica that I was taken to the building across the street from the gasoline station, across the street from the hotel, so I would establish contact with Mr. Jukic. I imagine that that is where their headquarters was. Before that, whether it was at the hotel or wherever, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that you were not very familiar with their structure, and you keep insisting on that; you've told us that several times. Now you mentioned brigade military police. Who's that?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is terminology that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina uses, and every unit, every bigger unit, like a brigade, has its own military police, and I imagine that that brigade also had its military police. I don't know. I'm telling you once again, please, don't take my word for it. I'm not familiar with the terminology either. I know there was a military police, but whether it belonged to the municipal staff or to the brigade or something else, I really don't know. I also know that there was another institution of the military police that was headed by Mr. Pasko Ljubicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, I'm going to stop you. Cross-examination of this witness about the other side, as it were, I don't think is going to take us much further, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I just got what I wanted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the Vitezovi. You mentioned the Vitezovi explicitly. You also mentioned that they came to your house twice before you were finally arrested a couple of days later. Without any further comment, do you know who their commander was?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I assumed that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, if you believe that that's it?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that you saw them from your window at the Cafe Benz, that they met there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let us not waste too much time now, but I would like to remind you that in the statement you made to the court in Zenica on the 3rd of October, 1994, you mentioned, as a place where the Vitezovi gathered, a cafe called "072" in the street of Petar Mecava. Are we perhaps talking about the same cafe or are these two different cafes?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, 072 is just below Benz. It's a different cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, these are places where the Vitezovi would gather?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were in Benz. Slavan Kraljevic continued after the war to use that shop as his own, although it's not really his.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Finally, on the 19th of April, 1994, you were arrested by a member of that unit and taken to the cinema where you were interned?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You told us that this was Rados Drazenko?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Rados Drazenko, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you know then that he belonged to the Vitezovi or did you find that out later?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: It said so on his arm band.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you knew that from the very outset, from that very event?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Until then, he was a member of the civilian police, as far as I know. He worked with me before we were driven out. He was a communications officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just one more thing in connection with this. From the 16th until the 19th of April, 1993, basically, they came to your house four times, and on the fourth time, you were interned and taken to the cinema. Out of those four times, on two occasions, you mentioned that these were specifically Vitezovi, and as far as these other two occasions were concerned, you just mentioned this general term "HVO." Can you identify on these two other occasions, which unit of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell us, who was it?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: The first time, it was colleagues, policemen from the Public Security Station, but they all had insignia of the Croatian Defence Council, that is to say, that the civilian police also had HVO insignia. Marko Rajkovic, he led that group, and Bonic, they are still working there at the police station as traffic policemen, and then Marko Rajkovic is working together with me until the present day, and I don't know about the third one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So they were from the civilian police but it was obvious that they belonged to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, because they wore those insignia, that is to say, they were members of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is exactly what I said. So now we've resolved the question of three of these occasions. What about the fourth time? What unit was it then?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Again, it was members of the HVO, but I don't know those men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So we're talking about this fourth occasion?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, we're talking about the third one, and I would like to thank them, even on this occasion, for the fairness they exhibited then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. So you cannot identify the persons who were there on the third occasion, so they were fair or -- well, not to say "kind," but they were fair?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Oh, yes, I give them all credit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was a very painful experience, and I do not want to remind you of that. Please understand me, I mean, as a Defence counsel, I have to ask those questions. A very simple question related to the killing of your brother and your sister-in-law. Did I understand you well that you all heard it from the mother of your brother's wife?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. Another question: They were murdered by members of the Vitezovi; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, a 70-year-old woman would hardly know who are the Vitezovi and who are the Croatian Defence Council or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But did you then learn subsequently which unit it was?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, had I learnt something, I suppose I would have said it in my statement or written it down in my documents in order to facilitate the task of the gentlemen of the Tribunal to bring the murderers to justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you do not know which HVO unit that was?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zlotrg, when, at long last, you were released from the place -- from the cinema, from where you were interned, you went to Zenica a little later on. Is it true that in Zenica you then began to work as a member of the commission for the exchange and release in the territory of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You were never a member of the commission for exchange?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the commission, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But did you try in any way whatsoever, try to help the exchange, because they became quite a frequent occurrence among the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: On two occasions only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And on one of those occasions, did you intercede on behalf of Dr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, we have now mentioned the place where you were interned, the cinema, or the Workers' University, as it was called, and you said that it was on the day when you were brought to the cinema, which was the 19th of April, 1993, that there were about 300 or 400 people all together, and that was as far as you could judge? Now, if the Court would allow me, before I tender this document, I should really like to read from a document. This is part of the supporting material and is marked with "Annex R," a page number given by the Registry, 1314, and this is a survey of events. This annex is a part of the report of a witness we shall be hearing from in a couple of days' time, Mr. McLeod. On page 5 of the report, on the 19th of April, 1993, the site Vitez, he says: "The ECMM visited the prison or, rather, the place of detention in Vitez where there were 62 Muslim males," detainees, that is. The first question: Is it true that in that basement, in the cellar of the Workers' University, only men were kept?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: When I came, yes. Before that, they also brought children and women there, and then they released them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then they released them?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not immediately. They released them after a day or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. Let's leave that. But when you arrived, there were only men there?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we can save a minute or two if -- perhaps we can save a minute if I mention the document that underlies this report, and then we shall tender it. This is a statement by Hendrik Morsink, a witness statement given to the Tribunal investigators between the 4th to 18th of December, '96. On page 5, he writes about the same visit to the Workers' University and says: "We also visited Muslim detainees in the cellar of the HVO headquarters, and I counted 62 of them there. It seems that they were treated well. They could receive visits from their family members."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Now, I should like to tender both these documents, of course, only the first page and the relevant page, because that is the document that can be found in the supporting material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The first statement, which comes from Mr. McLeod, had better be produced when he gives evidence. This witness doesn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I entirely agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It seems to me that it's the same with the second statement which you have. I don't think it's appropriate to produce it through this witness. He knows nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Of course, I entirely agree with that. I only wanted for everybody to see what I was citing from. However, there might be a problem if they do not appear as witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we will deal with that when it happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: During the direct examination, you said at some point that members of the Territorial Defence were called to report for labour duty. I think it was when you described 1992. Could you please explain, at least roughly, what does this labour obligation mean? What was under the then legislation? What was our duty as citizens then, just briefly, just in a few words?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, one does know what labour obligation is. It means that you have to come to work. Otherwise, you lose the status of an employee in a particular organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the authorities did have some legal grounds on the basis of which it could call people to respond to their labour duty?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Don't ask me that, ask somebody else. I don't really know whether there were legal grounds for that or not. But presumably there were, because they did call people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But did you ever get a summons to respond to a labour obligation?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: For Christ's sake, I was a member of the police. Police works always.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, we set up a police station, and of course we were doing our duty, and so my labour obligation would be with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. But does that mean that the authorities begin to assign you to different places? Some are assigned to military duty and some to labour duty; is that so?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you were one of those who did not have any labour duty because you were with the police, and you would be with the police even in case of war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is what the witness has said, at least so far as the first part is concerned. Can we slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, when you told us about when you were taken under custody, when they came to your house for the fourth time, and you used the word in Croatian, or rather in Bosniak or Serbian or Croatian, whichever language was spoken there, you used the word "arrested," as a police member, could you tell us, what does it mean, "arrested", and what is the difference between that and being taken under custody?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Persons who are taken under custody make a statement and go back home, and persons who are arrested, they unfortunately remain in detention; that is, in gaol, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is that the police definition? That is police terminology?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And when a person is arrested, mustn't he give a statement?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Under normal circumstances, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the word "interned"?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: During my stay in Vitez, no. I mean within those military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You heard it used then?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, no. I was arrested. They did not intern me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I did not understand you. Perhaps I got it wrong. The question was whether you have ever heard of the term "interned".

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but they did not use it when they arrested us. They did not use that term.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: By "they", whom do you mean?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Members of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you do know that in the nation -- a detainee and things, have you perhaps heard it from foreigners?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I remember hearing it before, but during that period of time, I never heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When you were, as you put it, arrested, you were taken to a camp, you said, and the word used in English is "camp". Is the place of your internment which you described -- could you describe it as a camp or as a place of detention?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, which place is that? Is that earlier on or at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, that is as soon as they came to the cinema building or Radnicki Univerzitet building, also called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And you're asking whether that could be called a camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, because the witness used that. It was translated correctly. He said "logor" in our language, which means, in English, "camp", and I don't think it is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Zlotrg, in a few words, would you describe it as a camp?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is how I perceived it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you another thing. In your earlier statements, again the one of the 3rd of October, '94, to the court in Zenica, you said then -- you say the place that all militarily-abled men were taken to, collection centres?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, aged between 15 to almost 70 years of age. There were all men there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you used the words "collection centre" here?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is something that one found written later, but the place where I was detained, I perceived it as a camp, and to my mind, that was a camp. We had no rights there, and members of the Croatian Defence Council could enter the rooms we were held in at any moment to tell us how they were killing, slaughtering, torching balija property and nobody ever tried to stop them. Had it been a collection or reception centre or prison, they wouldn't have been able to do that, because prison guards would have stopped them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But please, Witness, not in a single statement that you made nor during your testimony here did you say that there was any ill treatment in the cinema, in the workers' building, and now you implied it, although I'm not quite sure whether you are talking about the cinema, or Kaonik, or the Bungalow and so on and so forth. So was there any ill treatment in the cinema; did you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not physically, but Croatian [indiscernible] Centre is day and night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No. Please tell us, did anybody physically abuse you when you came to the cinema? Did you see anything of that kind when you came there?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not say that that happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When you were taken out to the Bungalow for the first time, and from there you went to Kaonik, did the military who took you out have any visible insignia? Could you tell us who that was?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it was the military police who guarded us, and I guess that it was they who took us away. But to begin with, it was night-time. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But in [indiscernible], you also told us it was military police there?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That was the command of Mr. Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the military police accounted to?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were accountable -- I mean that was the regional military police, as we might call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From Kaonik, you also said, or if I understood you well, that it was the military police who took you away?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't think that anybody else could have done that, because they took us here and there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, going back to that part when we talked about the digging of trenches, as an average citizen with minimum military duty, when does an army dig trenches, when it attacks or when it defends itself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a question for the witness. It's a question for us or a military expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could I rephrase?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Something else, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You told us, again in relation to those trenches, that some did not come back from digging them, that you did not eyewitness the death of anyone. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but we have heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you heard?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, naturally. And when I came out, it was all confirmed, and dead bodies were brought.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. Let me ask you something else. You mentioned Mehmed Sivro, your relative, and you said that you had also heard that he had not come back from digging; is that true?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, when I was at Kaonik. The first time that I was at Kaonik is when I heard this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But later on, you met him alive?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Also when we were exchanged. That means later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In other words, what you heard was only rumour? You did not see, with your own eyes, those events?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but when I met those relatives -- I also met parents of those young men who were killed, who never came back from the digging of trenches, and that was the confirmation of those rumours, and that is why I said that in my report. Otherwise, I would have said that those were rumours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us then go back to your final internment in the cinema; after Kaonik, when you went back to the cinema again. You told the court in Zenica that when you came out of the cinema at long last, you came out because Zjelko Sajevic put you in his car and took you home, to your home?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it was on the 30th of April, not when I was brought back from Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it was when you were released once and then came back?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, Sajevic took you from the cinema and gave you a lift home? That is what you said in the statement?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but before that I had to sign at so and so that I was leaving free and of my own free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you signed that. He took you home?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you said that the door was locked. What did he do?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: The gate -- the entrance door was locked, and he waited until one of the residents came down to unlock it. And only when I was in safely, he turned back to his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you it was for your safety?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let us go back, then, to those early days before they took you to the Workers' University, and then those visits home and so on and so forth. You said, at some point, that to one of those who came to see you, you said, "I will be safer if you took me to the cinema." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, from those two things that we just mentioned, could I draw the conclusion that it was dangerous for people in the town, especially if they were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. In the evening, they come and just take you away. And if you are locked up, they cannot reach you, so they cannot harm you, they cannot kill you, without knowing who that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it was safer in internment than outside?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us, when you were last released, that you had that conversation with Cerkez, and you said how you perceived that conversation. But does the fact remain that Cerkez used the following words, that you were not released for the purpose of your own safety?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot quote him, but no, no, that they were holding us there for our own safety because they had to show us to this commission of the BH army, and it's better for us to be safe and sound because they were responsible for the 30 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you recall that Ivica Santic was there to talk to the detainees and Skopljak Marijan?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Before Cerkez came, I think that was the day before Cerkez came, I know that Ivica Santic was there for sure. And whether Marijan was there or not, that I don't know, but if he had accompanied him, then he probably was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of that visit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you allow time for the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's been one or two occasions when I think there has been a problem with question and answer. There is one routine, and I don't know if it's going to help at all with problems of this type in this Chamber, where if there are two interpreters in a booth, one can do the question and one can do the answer, and that helps. I was looking at a previous passage with a problem about whether something was a question or an answer, I think. I didn't want to interrupt, because if those taking the notes are able to keep up, I didn't want to interrupt. But there have been one or two problems, I think, on the transcript this afternoon, from the speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The first thing is to allow time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, but sometimes you just have to go further. (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to this. Can you describe this to us? Was it clear why Mr. Santic came, regardless of whether Mr. Skopljak was there or not?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you how it was. Approximately, it was that there was the possibility of coexistence between the Croats and the Muslims and that the crimes that were committed were committed by members of the armed forces and that it is not the civilian government that had anything to do with it. That was his interpretation of events. But we did not agree to that, most of us. And then Mario Cerkez came the next day to continue along those lines, and I really cannot remember whether somebody else came between the two of them, I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You and I know this, but for the sake of the Court and the others who are listening, Ivica Santic was a civilian; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. If there was a civilian government at the time, everybody knew where the Croatian Defence Council was, and that is to say that they were supposed to have a command function over the army, and we see here that that did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is your opinion, but you do not know that for a fact, do you?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Santic, himself, said that this was done by members of the Croatian units, that the civilian government had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So there is a civilian government and there is a military government; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is what he said when he talked to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now you said to us that Cerkez continued the conversation along those lines?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to recall Z245. That is the document that is actually the agreement signed in Ahmici on the surrender of arms on the 22nd of October, 1992. Could you please tell the Court, how did this agreement come about on the 22nd of October? It was obviously a consequence of something.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know for sure, but I assume that most probably this was due to the events that took place in Novi Travnik before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This has nothing to do with the events that occurred when the main road was blocked, the one that passes by Ahmici, on the 19th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it is related to the events in Travnik, because the units of the HVO from Kiseljak, Busovaca and Kresevo went to help the HVO units in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know for sure that HVO units wanted to pass to Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, and from the contact I had with officers of the army, that's the way it was. But I don't know it for sure. You will have to ask someone from the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the army yourself now, so in October, there was an army, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Please, don't take my word for this terminology. When I say "army", I'm talking about the forces that were loyal to the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the president or the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and, rather, the president of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And may I remind you that in the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were two Croats as well, to the best of my knowledge. This is a long time ago. I don't know, perhaps I'm making a mistake now. So whenever I say members of the army, I'm actually thinking of those units that are loyal to the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Whether it was called the TO then, or the army, or the military, or -- I don't know. That's not important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Since you already mentioned this, that is to say, units that were loyal to the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the basis of the decision of the presidency as far back as July, the HVO was also a legal organisation, one of the two components of the armed forces of the republic?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And in '93, in April, they were also a legal component, and on the 15th, they were there to commemorate the holiday of the army in Stari Vitez in the headquarters of the Territorial Defence. Even when they committed a crime, they were a legal component. And in 1993, in July, they were also a legal component of the army, and also in Tuzla, in Kakanj, in Zepce?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: They remained armed because the army had armed them, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, I asked you this because of another thing. You said those who were loyal or who were not loyal. Obviously, that is not a criterion, and you said yourself there was this so-called Territorial Defence, and later on there was the army. And you said one thing, and you said that you didn't know when the Territorial Defence grew into the army, and we accepted that. But a few minutes ago, you said those army units that were loyal and under the command of the appropriate headquarters or the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that was the HVO, too?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Also the 16th of April, 1993, when they committed the crime, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So only on the 16th of April, 1993, there was this disruption?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Only with this part -- I mean where they had made this entity. But take the HVO of Kiseljak before they left, take the HVO of Tuzla. Throughout the war, it was a component of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And members of the Croatian Defence Council throughout the war came to Zenica with the insignia of the HVO, and nobody touched them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us go back to this document. You said that the road was blocked to HVO units, and you think that they were going to Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that the road was blocked. I think, but I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember at the time there was a lot of fighting going on around Jajce, where the Muslims and Croats together were trying to protect Jajce from the Serbs and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but I think that now we are really encumbering the Trial Chamber with things that don't really concern me. I'm a member of the police. I don't know the army very well, but as far as I know, every unit has to be announced to the units that hold the territory through which they are supposed to pass. If they were going to Jajce, then they were supposed to know that. The TO headquarters were supposed to know that they were supposed to pass to Jajce. But don't ask me about these military matters. I'm not an expert in military affairs, and I'm not here to give answers in that connection. I'm here to talk about things related to the police and those dates that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I have to correct you because you're hear to answer everything that you know about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I'm going to interrupt. Mr. Zlotrg, would you please answer the questions you're asked, if you can. If we don't think it's right that you should be asked, we will stop the witness. Mr. Kovacic, I wonder if there's much point asking this witness about this particular document. There will, I understand, be witnesses from Ahmici who may be in a better position to deal with it and also military witnesses who may be able to deal with it better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Certainly, there will be good witnesses. I just wanted to put this document into the context of events because it came here just out of the blue. There was an agreement, but it was obviously the result of something. I just wanted to confirm that, and, of course, we're going to question other witnesses about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just a small detail, please. When we were watching that video related to the bomb planted under the Salkic house, that was Z2559, do you know the physician who was there? You said this was a physician. Was this Mr. Gordon Peher?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. So you don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, I can take a break now. You said that you would like to take a break at a quarter past four. I'll be moving on to another subject, so if this is a good time for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. How much longer do you think you might be?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm now quite sure that I will be finishing with him in 30 minutes to 45 minutes at most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Good. Thank you. A quarter of an hour then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, let us finish the subject of internment, only a couple of short questions. While you were detained in the building of the Workers' University, that is, the cinema, did a physician come to visit?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that some asked for examination, but I didn't go to a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you did not receive the visit of any physician?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And in the chess club?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the chess club, nobody even knew we existed there, so they surely did not bring any physicians there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But was somebody taken out of the chess club for medical help?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to another subject. You said something about the television station belonging to Pero Gudelj and how the HVO took that station. Let us try and check some details about that. Could you, generally speaking, tell me, how were the citizens of the Vitez municipality informed? What could you listen to? Did you get the press regularly?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: The state television, the press arrived. I don't know whose -- I had no time to buy any newspapers because I had other duties, and I also watched private television, Mr. Gudelj's television.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you had the television programme of TV Sarajevo. There was the private television belonging to Pero Gudelj. Was there some other private station?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not at the beginning. Later on, there was the television of the war presidency, I don't know what it was called, out of the town of Vitez, but it worked for a very short while, and its ratings were very low.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know what transmitter, what relays were used to broadcast the programme? The transmitter for the signal into the Lasva Valley, where was it?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was on Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the transmitter above Tesic next to Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but that was a small transmitter which was simply used to amplify the signal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But in Vitez, could you watch television if that transmitter was out of work?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I could not tell you that. I only know that throughout the time we had the programme of the radio/television of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the radio/television of Mr. Gudelj's. At least in the part of the town where I lived, those were the only two stations we could watch, the first and second channel of the television of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the other one, the private one, when did it begin to work? Was it the television where Suad Salkic was the main man? Was that the television that you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't really know who was the main person there, because I could not watch it because the signal did not cover the part of the town where I lived. I did hear that they were broadcasting some programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday or, rather, on Thursday, the last working day last week, sometime toward the end of your testimony, you told us about the event when you met Cerkez in relation to the coffee shop owned by Dragan Cickovic. Are you sure it belonged to Dragan?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: The coffee shop is owned by Dragan's brother, Gojko, who had gone to Belgrade. Whether for reasons of health, that is, his wife's, because I know that she was ill for a long time, or whether he left for political reasons, I wouldn't know that. But I know that he left it to his brother Dragan to run it, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So Dragan Cickovic was looking after the coffee shop of his brother Gojko?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Have you heard that Dragan joined the Chetniks and that he called his people from the Chetnik side?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't know that, but I know that he moves about in Vitez freely now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is he the owner of the coffee shop again?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that last year it was returned to his brother. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But on that occasion or subsequently, since you were in the police, did you hear of any agreement between the HVO and Dragan about the taking over of that coffee shop?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I can read to you what Dragan told me. Because I could not remember the date when I had this conversation with Dragan, and then he told me that it was, I believe, on the 18th of May, and then what I stated, when Mr. Cerkez told him that the coffee shop was being mobilised. That is what I knew. Dragan never told me about any agreement. And even had there been any agreement, I wouldn't see any reason for 10 or 15 soldiers to go there to take over the coffee shop by agreement, by mutual consent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, when you came and saw those HVO soldiers, you approached an HVO policeman, your former -- could you conclude from anything when you had arrived at the time that something was happening, that something was going on, that an event was under way?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Members of the reserve police force were deployed around the coffee shop, and that was that. I did not really see members of the HVO. They must have been inside the coffee shop. I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But as you were there really when the event was taking place, did you see that any explosive device had been used or perhaps whether there was a threat that it would be used?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Since at that time we worked together, that is, we had one integrated police station, the station received no report of that kind. That is one thing. Secondly, members of the reserve police force wouldn't have come out for the investigation. It would have been the members of the crime investigation department or the [indiscernible] activity inspector would have come to remove that explosive device and authorise law enforcement officers, that is, professional people, rather than reserve police and Croatian Defence Council. Because, I'm telling you, the police at that time worked together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you are assuming that had there been a threat or an explosive device, that it would have been done by the proper police?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, because it was a civilian outlet, the civilian police, so the report was made to the civilian police, and we would have known it, but there was nothing. There was no application, no report to the Public Security Station about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Only one question more, Witness, and that will be it or, rather, I have several questions in relation to a subject. Is it true that during 1992, shifts went from Vitez to Vlasic to fight against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, not Vlasic alone, to Visoko. Members went to Visoko, to Bijelo Buce, to Vlasic too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: HVO units went to Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Who went where, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me rephrase it. So the units of the Territorial Defence and the units of the HVO went to some points of defence contracting Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that is correct. In view of this chaos in the town and the various incidents that you told us about, and we talked about the distribution of competencies or, rather, division of competencies between the civilian and military police, as a policeman, how did you treat an event in which an HVO soldier returning from his shift to his village, the town of Vitez, what was he if he committed a crime? Was he a civilian or was he a soldier?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: A soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the moment he arrived in his village from his shift, he was a civilian?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, if he was mobilised, then it would be natural for him to be a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No. But when you had TO shifts or HVO, it doesn't really matter because they belong to the same force, and when those units went to those places on the front against the Serbs, those soldiers were mobilised for a particular shift, I don't know, seven days, ten days, fourteen days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: You will have to ask that of one of the commanders or somebody in the secretariat for national defence. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Then didn't you face a problem to distinguish between civilians and military? If you didn't know that, how could you then differentiate between the competencies when conducting an investigation?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, we maintained permanent contact with the army, and if it wasn't under their jurisdiction, then we worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to '92.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: In '92, we also helped. In 1992, both components had their military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So, you would ask them, "Is this man a soldier or a civilian"; is that so?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think I already answered, that I wasn't assigning any investigation team. There was the law enforcement officer on duty there. So after a civilian report, he would have to send a police patrol to the scene of the crime to see what it was all about, and then when coming back with the report, then the law enforcement officer on duty would assign a team. If I was assigned to that particular team, then it meant that that particular incident came under my jurisdiction. And if I would be called by somebody from the military police, then it meant that it was under their jurisdiction, but since they lacked technicians, I would be simply doing a service to them. But it wasn't up to me to determine to define the event. There was the law enforcement officer on duty who decided that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell us, is a uniform an element whereby you can distinguish between a soldier and a civilian, say as of mid-1992, or not?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, anybody could wear a camouflage uniform. Whoever could afford it could buy it and therefore wear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But could we say that people wore uniforms as a rule?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So regardless of whether they did belong to an army or not?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I think we're talking at cross-purposes. I thought you were talking about members of the military, if they wore uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, I mean all.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were also members of the army who were in civilians, because the army did not have enough uniforms. So it was not a rule, really, it was his military card, whether to see a document which showed whether somebody was a member of a unit or not. The uniform was worn by those who had them. I think that is how it is today. I mean you have your identity card or your military card to show whether you were a member belonging to a unit or whether you were a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you're saying that a military person can also wear civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Zlotrg, thank you very much for the answers. Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, my name is Bob Stein. I live in New Hampshire in the United States. It's my pleasure and privilege to represent Dario Kordic. If there's any question that I ask you that you don't understand, will you let me know? And you have to say "Yes" or "No" for the record. All right?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You have to say it.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Sir, in addition to your appearance in October of 1994 in the court in Zenica, you also gave a series of other interviews with the Prosecution; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And indeed before you gave those interviews, you had prepared some notes, which we have, that you prepared on June 5, 1996. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Actually, I think the transcriptist made a mistake when she transcribed those or translated those notes. Those notes were actually made or compiled by you on September 5, 1996. Does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it's the 5th of September, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. And then, as I understand it, you submitted to an interview on June 10, 1997, by some people from the Office of the Prosecution. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not by the date, but I talked to the Prosecutors on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It could have been the summer of 1997?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And then again in the fall of 1998, on September 27 and 28, again you had a discussion with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And then you testified in the Kupreskic case in October of 1998. Do you recall coming here and testifying?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And before that testimony, you spoke again with members of the Prosecution; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Certainly, you didn't just come in to The Hague and take the witness stand. You spoke with members of the Prosecution team; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
