utterances.text: Yes. I do not recall the date, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. The record shows that the testimony was on October 14 and October 15, 1998. So the fall of 1998, you met with members of the Kupreskic prosecution team; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: For several days?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Until we finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: How many days was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: More than one?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had so many different conversations with them that I really cannot remember how many days I actually spent there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. And then again on March 4, 1998, you testified in the Aleksovski case?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And again you spent some time with the Prosecutors then; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And then last, or next to last, I guess, you were interviewed again in November of 1998, after your testimony in Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I already said it, I talked to them on several occasions, but I don't know the dates. I don't know. If that's what it says over there, then that's probably what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. And again in February of 1999, February 4?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, if that's what it says there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And on all those occasions, you told the truth?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And on all those occasions, you answered any of the questions the Prosecutors put to you relative to the events that you knew of; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: They asked you questions about all of the defendants, including my client, Mr. Kordic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I don't have much to say about Kordic, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: But you told them everything you did have to say about Mr. Kordic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, do I also understand that there came a period in time where you interviewed detainees at the detention centre in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And that was in connection with your police report, your police work?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Detainees were Croats, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but at that time I was not a member of the Ministry of the Interior. I was mobilised. I was a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. So as a member of the army, you interviewed Croats at the detention centre in Zenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And that was in 1993?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Do I also understand that you participated in helping various individuals from your community who were to testify here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, please, sir, to take a look at Exhibit number 332,1. I would like you to have the Croatian version. The notes before you at Exhibit Z332,1 are not writings that you, yourself, made; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't write any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: They were all written by someone else?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: This was taken out of the complaints book of the police station at Stari Vitez, and I have the original, if necessary. I have the original here with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: They were not taken out by you, were they, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The person who took these notes from the police book was not you?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I gave this to the Office of the Prosecutor to copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And you got this from someone else?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Took it from the station, from the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: But you didn't bring the entire book with you, did you?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: This is all there is in the book, these pages?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, from the 23rd of December until the 14th of April, 1993, but only what the criminal police recorded, not everything that was recorded by the Public Security Station.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So there's another set of notes recorded by the Public Security Station; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You are telling us that 332,1, these documents, is a complete record of the police activity; is that right? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: This document records the time and location of events that took place and the person who reported on this, and it should also reflect who received this report. And I noticed in the first two, there was no signature of who had received this, and then you have "Alihodza Sejo", "Alihodza Sejo" afterwards. He was acting chief of the crime police in Stari Vitez. You have his name here, Alihodza Sejo, Alihodza Sejo, on the 23rd, for example, of December, 1992, at the premises of the Public Security Station in Stari Vitez, Handija Handzic [indiscernible]. That is to say, he had all the particulars of the person who was reporting the event; that is to say, what was done, what the damages incurred were, et cetera. Then on that basis, we were supposed to carry out an on-site investigation. If possible, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I understand, sir, but that's not my question. Are these notes all there is in that police record?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's not a record, it is a book. It's a book of complaints of citizens in respect of things that were done to them. So it is just that they lodge a complaint, and then it is up to us to see whether we were in charge or not, and then that would be within the domain of the crime police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: A simple question. Is everything that's in the book here today or not?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. No, no. That which is not of interest to this court -- sorry, sorry. The entire book was photocopied. It's different in my statement, though. So everything that is in the original is here, photocopied.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That is my question.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's it. This is the original version, and everything that is there has been photocopied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Stein, I believe that if you want to have a clear discussion, we have to clarify certain things, because the further it goes, the messier it becomes. I believe the witness is telling us that all the police records, the daily reports made by individuals, are put in a document which is an ordinary, usual document in which everything that happens in a police station is recorded. Could you ask the witness whether the document that we have in front of us is a comprehensive document for a given period of time, whether it covers everything that happened during that specific period? Obviously enough, there is other information, but that's what we need to clarify. There may be other information for other periods of time, but as far as this period is concerned, do we have the entire document, because we fail to understand so far. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, did you hear the Judge's question? For the period of time between December 23, 1992, and February -- well, actually, it would be April, 1993, would you explain first how your police department keeps records of citizens' complaints, and then, second, is this the complete record? I believe that's the Judge's question.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Since we had just established the police station, that is to say that we did not have all the original forms then, we simply established this notebook which had a stamp on it, and all the citizens' complaints are in there. However, when someone starts working on a case on the basis of a citizen's complaint, then a file is opened, then a record is made, then this is typed out, and that is what is in the file. So this is only what the citizens reported to us, in terms of what happened, and everything else that was done in this connection is in the file that is for each and every particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So the citizen would come in and make a report, correct, and that would be put in your book?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. They dictated orally to the person who was actually writing this down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes. If that complaint was later investigated by your department, those were in different documents; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, then the file is opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: But these complaints during the period of time I mentioned, December through April, are all the complaints that exist; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were other reports that were filed in the book that was kept by the policeman on duty, because there was a policeman that was on duty around the clock and we were there only for eight hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Is this the book that was kept round the clock?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, this is the book that was kept by the crime police, only that department within the police station. That is to say when we were at work, then we would receive the report directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge Bennouna, I'm afraid I haven't clarified it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stein, I think we've got it as clear as we're going to get it, if you would like to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: What I would like to do, then, is turn your attention, please, to the notes, which I would like to have admitted at this point in time. And those would be the notes provided by the Prosecutor from 5 June, '96, about events in Vitez from 1991 until 16 May, '93.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be marked D15/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, I would like to turn your attention to the English version at page 17, and the Croatian version would begin on page 3. These are notes prepared by you about events in Vitez from 1991 until 16 May, 1993, are they not?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: At which page, Mr. Stein? We've got no pagination, apart from a general pagination at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, Sir. It's probably cut off. The page I'm referring to would be base number 607788.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we've got that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, in this document you set out complaints by citizens to your police department; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The same kind of complaints we just talked about?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but it need not be recorded in this photocopy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: These dates of the complaints, starting at your version, page 3, and the English version at page 17, or base number 607788, are different complaints, are they not?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And you also have a personal journal, do you not?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, I took your answer, and I went back over the record. You testified earlier, "Secondly, as I have said, I had my journal, and I noted down all those events, and also in the archives of the police department, you can find these events recorded." Is there a separate journal from those which are in the archives of the police department which you have in your possession?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I had a logbook where I simply put in every time I went out to the scene of the reported crime. However, during military operations in Stari Vitez, that logbook was destroyed, and I never laid my hands again on it, because if it were still in existence, there would be much more about it here, more individual incidents and, of course, greater detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The notes that you wrote on June 5 or September 5, 1996, now Exhibit D15/1, where did those notes come from?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: My memory, citizens' reports, complaints, military police notes, which worked in the same building as the civilian police, and some other documents. I cannot recall them. I do have here a couple of statements. Perhaps if one of them is of particular interest to you, I can show it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And you have those notes with you in The Hague now?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have -- no, the original, the one that you gave me, that is not a statement which I gave to the Prosecutor of The Hague Tribunal. This was my official memo of what happened, and it was at my insistence, when the gentlemen came to me to take the statement for Mr. Aleksovski, I then offered him this -- well, this kind of a memo, these kinds of things that I was noting from '91 to the 16th of May, '94. The gentleman who came on that occasion on behalf of the Prosecution took that document from me, and I signed it. So I was the one who offered this document, and I made no statement in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So my question is, to be quite clear about this, the notes that you had during that interview and which you used during that interview, which are set out at D15/1, you turned over to the Prosecutor; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And those are different notes from the official police record which you had before you as 332,2; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is my version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Which you kept for your purposes?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not keep it. I took it later on from the archives of the police station, everything I thought that could be of interest and related to the events that took place during that period of time. It is all clear, I mean, dates and sites, and all that you have in the police station in Vitez must be the original document that is kept in the archives of the police. I do have something here, but that is not all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. So you selectively picked certain parts from the archives of the police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, because I was an active participant of these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And you chose what you'd give to the representative from the Prosecutor's office; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Therefore --

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: All that I knew about that period of time, and I believe you will agree with me that nobody can remember all those dates. So that is why I noted it down, and to write down the dates, I had to go into the archives to take them out. All the events, I don't have to read anything about them because I attended practically all the on-site investigations, and whenever citizens came with their complaints, I was usually there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I want to ask you about your memory right now. You testified earlier that you had an experience with a man named Cicko, not a very pleasant one, in which he was bragging. Do you recall that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Miroslav Bralo, Cicko.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You said in your testimony the other day, if I'm quoting it properly and I believe I am, that there was another person that was mentioned during that conversation named Svabo. Do you remember Svabo, the name "Svabo"?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: That person was not there. Cicko told us that he was vying with him who would kill more balijas. That is a derogatory name for Muslims. If I'm correct, Cicko mentioned 80 but perhaps less. At that time, it wasn't really particularly pleasant to stand before such a fiend, because he told us how he had crucified a man like Jesus Christ on a door, and any member of that group who dug trenches with me up there could confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, you specifically said that "His name is Svabo, and he is a member of the Croatian Defence Council from Busovaca. I did know his name but now I really can't remember it." That's what you told us last week. That's a direct quote from your testimony. Now, let me ask you this --

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. I would like you to take a look at D15/1, which is in front of you, I believe, your notes. Do you have those in front of you?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but just help me what it is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sure. Take a look at the Croatian version, and it appears to be at the top of page 9, number 005-09-017, and the English version would be page 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: If Your Honours don't have a full copy, that would be 006-07-786. I'm referring in the English to the second full paragraph and in the Croatian to the very sentence on the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Do you see the sentence? The English version reads as follows: "He bragged to us that he and another man from Busovaca were competing in who would kill the most Muslims. He said he was currently in the lead and that he had killed about 80 men and women and children." Have I read that correctly, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That statement was given again in your notes. That appears in your notes, your own handwritten version. Now, I'd like you to take a look at Exhibit 332,2. The English version of what I'm referring to is at page 12 and the Croatian is also at page 12. That's page 12, about three-quarters of the way down the Croatian version, and the English version, about halfway down. According to the English version, you said to the judge in Zenica: "After the introduction, Cicko began to brag that he and another soldier from Busovaca, whose name he mentioned but I cannot recall at the moment, were competing over who could kill, that is, slit the throats of more balijas." That's what it says there, doesn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I cannot really quote him, what he said exactly, but that is roughly what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The specific name "Svabo" does not appear in either one of your statements; correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not in this version. He probably didn't ask me -- the judge did not ask me, because I think we worked for two days so that -- but the fact is that he said his name, surname, the nickname "Svabo," and that's all. There were about 10 or 15 of us there who were there when he taught us how to make the sign the of cross, and that we were no longer Muslims but Catholics. One doesn't forget that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Of course not. One doesn't forget that, you didn't forget it, but you didn't mention his name on either of the prior occasions before you came into court today; correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it must be that nobody ever asked me or perhaps I could not remember his nickname at the time, but it says everywhere that he was competing with a Croat from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, sir, let me ask you this: You talked, in your direct examination, about some fuses and Pero Skopljak -- I'm not doing well on the name, I know -- and about a convoy. Do you remember that testimony a few days ago? None of that information you saw yourself; none of those events you saw with your own eyes; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All of those events were told to you by another person; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: I saw drivers at the Public Security Station when they came to report an armed robbery, because that is nothing else but a case of armed robbery. They seized two trucks by resorting to weapons. At that time, I did not know Mr. Skopljak. I learnt about him later from my colleague, who was with another fellow policeman, and he admitted as much. You can also ask Mr. Mirsad Tatarevic, because he told me in a conversation that there was no need for him to come to testify; otherwise, I wouldn't have mentioned his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let's be clear. Your information about who was the mastermind of that plot came from Mirsad Tatarevic, and he got it from another person named Ramljak; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Vlado Ramljak, a policeman who was ordered to do that by Pero Skopljak. That was how I always presented it. I never stated it any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And Vlado Ramljak was drinking with Mirsad Tatarevic when this whole conversation happened; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is information that I have. I don't know. I wasn't with them. That is what Mr. Tatarevic told me, and that is what I'm now transmitting to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We have an expression in the States called "whiskey talk," so I'll make this simple. Did you have any similar conversation with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has given his evidence about the way he received the information. It will be for us to evaluate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Believe it or not, I was trying to shorten the examination. I don't think it was going to be successful anyhow. Judge, I have maybe 20 more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn. Mr. Zlotrg, we're adjourning now. Could you be back, please, tomorrow afternoon at half past two, when your evidence will, in fact, be completed? If you would like to go now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, are there some matters you want to raise with regard to housekeeping and procedures?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Maybe one or two matters we can mention very briefly when the witness is gone, nothing to do with the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the immediately pressing or potentially pressing administrative matter to deal with is the timing of the search warrant argument, it having been suggested through the usual channels that the end of next week might be a possibility. The problem there is, of course, the problem both of readiness of both parties, and I understand informally that the Defence, who intend to call a couple of witnesses, would be ready then. I haven't finally confirmed with those on our side, but I'm pretty sure we will be ready to go ahead by then. But the competing interest is the interest of witnesses. Following this witness, there's a witness whose timetable is very tight, and we very much hope to start him tomorrow in order to complete him well before the end of the week. The next witness is a man called (redacted), who I was hoping to fit in at the end of this week, beginning of next, and then to have Mujezinovic, who was brought here and had to be sent back last week on a pretty certain starting time, maybe Tuesday or Wednesday of next week in order that he could be completed within the week. That was my plan. I know that these plans have to change from time to time. Indeed, they have to change pretty well daily as the timetable unfolds. If we put the interest of getting those witnesses through, then there might well not be enough time for the search warrant issue to be argued at the end of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me add this: We shall not be sitting Friday afternoon, as usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If Friday the 14th is not a convenient date, and I should say we are in the parties' hands as far as this is concerned, another possible date is Monday the 31st of May when we come back to start another session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Two points arising from that. First, when you say we shan't not be sitting on Friday afternoon, is that this week as well as next week?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that this week, we have four afternoons, and then next week, we have four and a half days. I think it's pretty unlikely that we will get through the witnesses I have lined up and have any time for the argument. I have some considerable concerns about whether we will get through Mujezinovic in the present order of things, and I may have to consider reversing him and (redacted) if his interests rank over 16 (redacted) his personal interests. I would have thought, frankly, that the 31st of May is a better option because it brings with it certainty, and we can probably line up the first witness thereafter for the day after the 1st of June with all sorts of flexibilities available, probably to bring him forward, if the argument only takes half a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That sounds like a sensible solution. If the Defence want to raise any matters about that, of course, they can. I understand that evidence will be called in the course of this argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to ask the Court what directions it's going to give about the exchange of summaries of any evidence to be called on behalf of the Defence. This is an interlocutory matter. I'm not sure if it's strictly governed by the terms of the order that you have made or intend to make in respect of Defence evidence, but I would see no reason why the same principle shouldn't apply for interlocutory matters, and, indeed, it's likely to help the satisfactory outcome of these applications if it's pretty well carved up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's certainly within the spirit of the practice here. It would assist, would it not, in clarifying the issues, any issues of fact which have to be decided between the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think at the moment it's a two-week order. As you will appreciate, from the Prosecution's point of view, we've well exceeded two weeks. We're serving witness statements and notifications now months in advance, but that's not necessarily going to have the same effect on the Defence. But I think a reasonable time limit would be very helpful and enable clarification of the issues which are otherwise probably reasonably fully argued or, as the phrase has it, briefed at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, because they were the subject of an extensive filing, as I remember, probably on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So they are already in written form. There is no need for any orders in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was a third filing by the Defence which I characterised as being effectively a reply, because it was brought in under another topic which didn't need an argument at all, so that it's very fully argued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So if we ordered that the hearing of the issue should take place on the 31st of May, you have disclosed your evidence on the topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, I don't think we've necessarily finally concluded that we are going to call evidence, but certainly if we're going to, we will disclose it as soon as we can. I'll go and discuss that with others more intimately concerned with this aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But you would be prepared to disclose any evidence two weeks beforehand, the 17th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And you would like us to make a similar order in relation to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, do you object to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Everything seems perfectly reasonable. The 31st is a grand idea. At this present time, we are not sure whether we will be calling two, one, or no witnesses, and we can comply with the orders just contemplated easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The order will be that both sides disclose summaries of any evidence they are going to call on the issue by the 17th of May or on the 17th of May. For the sake of clarity, the issue is evidence arising from -- the admissibility of evidence arising out of the execution of a search warrant in, was it, September of last year?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That can no doubt be noted for the purposes of drawing up an order, although I doubt we need one. It's quite clear what it is. Perhaps if someone would take it off the transcript, that would be sufficient. We will consider whether we need a scheduling order. It may be neater to have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I believe the matter is fully briefed, argued. You have all the papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. So effectively it may not take -- provided the issues are fairly narrow, the issues of fact, despite calling evidence, it may not take very long.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. That's why if we have the witness normally lined up for the Tuesday but in The Hague on the Sunday or even the previous Friday, then we can be ready to fill a gap if a gap appears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us say, optimistically, a time estimate of no more than half a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I think that's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Shall I just deal with one or two other matters at the moment? I gather that the days of the 20th and the 21st are likely to be occupied by matters that won't involve witnesses and won't involve the Defence, and I only mention this because it's been in my mind, I've mentioned it to Mr. Stein and I think it's probably in the Tribunal's mind, ex parte matters have somewhat grown, I think, in the Tribunal over recent months and years, and there are those who think that it's not a bad idea if one can have the maximum possible disclosure of what's going on by one party to the other, even when ex parte hearings are being held. I think it's probably something that the Registry is thinking about itself. It had occurred to me that it might be sensible in this trial, which is obviously going to last some time, to see if we can devise a regime of being as full, in the provision of details on the other side, as can be. I mention that Mr. Stein might, for example, say, "Well, we're having an ex parte hearing about," and then you can at least sometimes, if the Chamber approves, you can at least identify the topic. That makes the record that much more complete, and it avoids any slipshod ex parte practices from developing which one knows from other jurisdictions have sometimes occurred. I only mention that now. If we can think of a way of dealing with it, so much the better. Having said that, in relation to those two days, there may be something that we want to mention simply by way of timetabling. In line with the spirit of not having written motions for everything, if tomorrow I'd like to raise that ex parte at the end of the day, perhaps I'll be able to do it then. It will only be, I think, for timetabling or for what motions have to be served, but I don't want to do it now because I haven't clarified the thing with Ms. Featherstone and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It should be made plain that our proceedings are inter parte. That means that they take place in the presence of all and not one party and that ex parte proceedings, even if permitted, are to be kept to an absolute minimum. There are issues in this case which have to be dealt with ex parte. If at least the subject matter can be identified to the other side, and this will apply to both sides, so much the better because, in that way, it avoids any suspicion as to what might be going on in the absence of both parties. Mr. Nice, I would encourage the development, if possible, of a procedure which allows for as much disclosure as is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Then tomorrow I may find myself asking for five minutes to deal with a timetabling matter on an ex parte motion, the general nature of which I may be able to divulge. The next thing is, again in the spirit of there being no written motions or as few written motions as possible, at some stage, I want to apply to add to the witness list three names. They have already, in fact, been included in the latest document you've got in summary form. Can I take it that that's something that should be done in court or would you prefer that that matter be dealt with by written motion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will have to deal with it, but you refer to it in your latest document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's there, yes. It's under Zepce, I think. I'm afraid I don't have the page numbers at hand. I don't refer to the application. I refer to the content of the witness statements. It's on page 80 of the witness's -- I beg your pardon, page 81.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why don't you make this the application? What are their names or are you not in a position to do so?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I haven't prepared it as fully as I would have done, which is why I'm reluctant to make it right away. Page 81, and they are all marked. Perhaps if you would be good enough to consider the summaries overnight, then I can just deal with that more fully tomorrow morning. They are the three witnesses listed on page 81 and marked as "Additional Subject to Application." There's one other as well. It's better that I deal with it tomorrow. In any event, it's better that I deal with it when the Chamber has had an opportunity to consider the document that I served, as I promised I would serve today, or filed, as I promised I would file today, because it may be that even tomorrow -- being anxious not to cut into witness time, even tomorrow, the Court might want me to take it through the document if it is not self-explanatory, as I would hope it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are anxious to deal with this matter and get to grips with the number of witnesses and the extent of the evidence. That application should perhaps better be postponed until we are going to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I can tell you that we are meeting on Wednesday after the hearing to begin our work upon this topic. We would wish, as soon as possible thereafter, to go through the witnesses to get some sort of order into the matter, from our point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope you'll find this document helpful. I know you can't have any opportunity to look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It was handed to us as we came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I thought it probably was. It's passages of text with the existing revised witness summaries fitted in and characterised or categorised in two ways. The document is self-explanatory, and there's a discussion passage in the last three or four pages of the document, which I hope you'll find all provides a helpful starting point for the exercises that we all have to go through. The document may itself have to be subject to some revision, as is made clear in the opening passage, because the mission or, indeed, missions that have been underway and which I told you of, aimed at discovering in more detail witness availability and attitude, have only just returned. So only part of their feedback, if that's the right word, is included. They need to be fully debriefed by me later in the week, and, indeed, those taking part are entitled to contribute to the way that I have, in their absence to some degree, categorised the witnesses. So there may be some need for revision, but I think that basically this is a document that will set sails for the future. I trust that the Court has also had and its staff has been able to use the additional missing pages from the core bundle of documents. They were provided in a format that should have enabled your staff to fit them in to exactly the right place in the core documents, so that the core documents become if not absolutely complete, document by document, very nearly so. I think that's all the housekeeping I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: At the beginning of next week, you should be in the position to be up to date, presumably, having talked to the people who've come back with witness availability to tell us if there's any revision which can be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly by the beginning of next week. I can even give you some further provisional views before Wednesday, if that would help in the meeting that you're having then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you have any further information, let us know tomorrow or perhaps on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Obviously, the whole topic has to be discussed and, no doubt, argued about before any decisions are made and matters of principle to arise, but I have set them out in the discussion document at the end. Judge Bennouna, I don't know if it's in French yet. I suspect not, and I'm very sorry, but it was only in final form, I think, yesterday afternoon or this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. No, I didn't want to speak about the language, as such. I'm now slowly learning to accept the hard realities of this Tribunal being what it is, and I'm learning to accept, among others, this privilege which is given to one language rather than to another. We're learning to live with it and possibly learning to improve on our understanding of either language. This is not so bad after all maybe. Thank you, Mr. Kovacic, for thinking of me all the time. I'm very thankful to you for that. But don't worry, I'm able to follow what's happening in detail, in spite of it all. There was only one thing. I believe that it is the contents of this document which is interesting. It is good work that you've done there. We're going to be able to use this document. If I understand it well, you have ordered the witnesses, for which we now have their summaries, you've classed them or ordered them by locality and also by count in the indictment. In front of each witness, we have the locality, as well as the counts of the indictment; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Partly so. The categorisation is slightly more detailed than that. We've listed first those witnesses who can speak directly about the defendants or either of them, and we then divided that category of witnesses up into those who we categorise as essential, and we qualify that term, but essential and those who are less essential. If you look at page 4 of the bundle you have, you'll see the witness, numbered 2 elsewhere, named; you will see a bold line to the left of the page which signifies he's an essential witness, and you will see his evidence is, as in the revised summary, set out, although highlighted for your assistance with that which is plainly critical. Then you go over the page through page 5 and so on with the rest of this series of witnesses who can give direct evidence about the defendants. It happens that those witnesses cover a large number of counts as well, and therefore it was thought appropriate to mark and helpful to mark which counts they cover. So if we stay on page 5, as an example, and you look at the top witness, since I don't know what, if any, protection may be sought, I shan't give the name, but you can see the counts that are identified. If you look at the next witness, number 15, you'll see again the counts that are capable of being dealt with, but you'll see the word "unwilling" marked there, reflecting some of the information coming to us from the most recent exercises. So that throughout the first section, then you can go on to -- just to explain the format of the document, this is the largest section -- you go on until you get to page 24, and then between 23 and 24, it happens to fall on the top of the page, there's a thick horizontal line, and so you're now coming literally to the witnesses who are below the line who we categorise as less essential. They still are witnesses who are capable of covering, in specific terms, either Kordic or Cerkez, but they are, in our judgement, less essential. Now, that's the first category of witnesses, and it's the biggest. If you go to page 34, you find the beginning of the second category of witnesses, the international military personnel and monitors who had direct contact with Kordic and Cerkez, a very important set of witnesses. And we've pursued the same course there, starting with Witness 18. The strong line on the left-hand side enables you to know, even if you dip into the pages and don't know which section you're in, how the witness is categorised. It sets out again the counts that he can cover, and it sets out, in the summary of his evidence, by highlighting, what's the particularly critical features. The next section of witnesses begins -- and so again in this section you go on from those who are sidelined as important to those who are less. Then you come to page 47, which is experts and quasi-experts, similarly dealt with in terms of whether essential or not. At page 50, you come to those witnesses who deal with attacks on villages, and it's broken down then by localities, not by villages but by localities. And you can see the localities. And again the strength of the witnesses or their essential nature is distinguished by whether they have a bold line beside their name or not. That takes us to the end of the document, all but for the discussion that the Court specifically referred to when inviting us to provide this document, which starts at page 85 and is just really three or so sides of important points to be considered. I hope you'll find this a document that will both set out our thinking and our approach to the witnesses, and in the discussion document, identifies some of the thorny issues that we've simply got to grapple with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And how many essential witnesses have you identified?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's been renumbered in my absence over the weekend, and I think it comes between 100 and 150. Before you look at the questions of unwilling, it's about 150, page 3. But as you'll see from the discussion paper at the end, we're going to invite the Chamber to say that there is the real need in the Chamber, and the real potential in the Chamber, for introducing means by which more evidence can be properly received in a given time, and that that is the most important next step for this Chamber to take. May I simply say to Judge Bennouna, and I hope I'll be forgiven this late in the afternoon, I sympathise with him, and it's a matter of great regret, I think for many of us here in the institution, that in a bilingual institution, there aren't the facilities for those who would like to either improve or even those starting from scratch to become adept in both languages. Having made that point, it may even sound like a complaint, I say no more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, as to that, you must make your own arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn. Half past 2.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 5.51 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 4th day of May, 1999, at 2.30 p.m.
